text: You get an integer array called hand, and an integer called group size. Return true if you can split all the cards into groups. Each group has exactly group-size cards, and the values in a group are consecutive.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — every card must be used, and each card goes into exactly one group. A group like two, three, four is fine, but two, two, three is not. And the order of the cards in the hand doesn't matter, because I can rearrange them. Is that right?
Yes. All cards used, no repeats inside a group, and order doesn't matter.

Okay. Then only two things matter: which values I have, and how many copies of each. So I can think in counts, not in positions. And here's the key fact I want to plant early. Look at the smallest card that's left. It can't be in the middle of a group, because nothing smaller is left to come before it. So it must start a group. And if it has several copies — say count copies — every one of those copies must start its own group. Are there any constraints on the input size?
The hand has between one and ten to the fourth cards. Each card value is between zero and ten to the ninth. And group size is at least one, and at most the length of the hand.

Got it. The values go up to ten to the ninth, so I can't use a plain array indexed by value. I'll need a map. And later I'll be computing k plus i, so I'll keep overflow in mind. Let me run through the example. One, two, three, six, two, three, four, seven, eight, with a group size of three. The smallest card is one, so one starts a group: one, two, three. Now the smallest card left is two: two, three, four. Then six: six, seven, eight. All the cards are used, so the answer is true. The second example is one through five, with a group size of four. One starts the group one, two, three, four, and then five is left alone. It needs six, seven, and eight, and there's no six. So the answer is false.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. A naive approach would be to backtrack. Pick a card, try every way to build a group with it, and undo when I get stuck. That's exponential. With up to ten thousand cards, it won't finish. This problem reminds me of a greedy pass over a sorted count map. The fact from before removes all the choice. The smallest card has only one legal role, so there's nothing to try — I just follow it. And I don't need to build one group at a time, either. If the smallest value k has count copies, I start that many groups at once. That means I need the same number of copies of k, k plus one, and so on, up to k plus group size minus one. So I subtract that count from all of them in a single pass. I'll go with an ordered map from int to int. It gives me the counts, and it walks the keys from small to large for free.

Here's the plan. My state is a frequency map: for each value, how many copies are not used yet. And the invariant is: when I reach key k, every key smaller than k is already at zero. First I build the frequency map from the hand. Then I walk the keys in increasing order. For each key, I copy its count into a plain variable — a copy, not a reference. If that count is zero, the key was used up by earlier groups, so I skip it. Otherwise, for each offset i from zero up to group size minus one: if k plus i is missing, or it has fewer copies than count, I return false. If not, I subtract count from it. If I get through every key, I return true. Here, I'm using an ordered map to keep track of how many copies of each value are still free. Because the keys come out sorted, the key I'm on is always the smallest card still left. One thing worth flagging — the invariant is what makes the greedy safe. Let me walk through that. When I reach k, all the smaller keys are already zero. So the copies of k can't join any group that started earlier. They must start new groups. If any of k plus one through k plus group size minus one is short, there's no other way to place those cards. So returning false right away is correct, not just fast. There's a trade-off here. I could also sort the array and use a hash map. The ordered map costs log n per access. But it keeps the code short, and it gives me sorted keys without a separate sort. At ten thousand cards, that's fine. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. I'll think out loud as I go. I declare an ordered map called freq, and in the first loop I bump the count for every card in the hand. Then the second loop walks the map with a structured binding — the key k and its value v. Inside, I copy v into an int called count, and if count is zero I continue. Then the inner loop goes over i from zero to group size. If the map doesn't contain k plus i, or the count stored there is less than count, I return false. Otherwise I subtract count from it. After both loops, I return true. That matches the plan line by line. One thing worth flagging — copying v into count is needed for correctness. v is a reference to the map entry for k. When i is zero, the subtraction sets that entry to zero. If I used v directly, v would also become zero right there. Then every later check and subtraction for k plus one and up would use zero, and the groups would never really be taken out. Copying first freezes the number of groups I'm starting. Two more small details. The skip on zero is also needed. Keys that earlier groups used up are still in the map, just with zero. Without the skip, I'd try to start groups at those keys. Near the top end, a key like k plus one may not exist, so it could wrongly return false. And the order inside the if matters. The does-the-map-contain-this-key check runs first, and the or short-circuits. So the bracket lookup only runs when the key already exists. It never inserts a new key while I'm walking the map. In my tests, the map size never changed.

Let's dry-run the code with an example. Example one: one, two, three, six, two, three, four, seven, eight, with group size three. Expected true. After the first loop, one has one copy, two and three have two copies each, and four, six, seven and eight have one each. At key one, count is one, so I take out one, two, three. Key two drops to one copy. The key row is key two. It started with two copies, but the group at one already used one. So count is one, and I start only one group here: two, three, four, which takes all three of them to zero. That's the invariant at work — when I reach two, key one is already zero. Then keys three and four show up with zero, and the skip handles them. Key six takes out six, seven, eight, and now everything is zero. Seven and eight get skipped, and I return true. In total, four keys get skipped: three, four, seven, and eight. Example two: one through five, with size four. At key one, count is one, so one through four all go from one to zero. Keys two, three and four are skipped. At key five, count is one, five goes to zero, and then key six is missing. Return false. Correct. I also want one case where count is bigger than one. One, one, two, two, three, three, three, four, five, with size three. At key one, count is two, so I start two groups at once. One goes from two to zero, two goes from two to zero, and three goes from three to one. Key two is skipped. At key three, count is one: three, four, and five all go to zero. Keys four and five are skipped. Return true. This is the case where the copy really earns its place. Let's also test with corner cases. With a group size of one, every card is its own group. The inner loop runs once and subtracts the full count. Always true. Five, five, five, with size three: count is three, five goes from three to zero, then key six is missing. False — three copies of one value can't be consecutive. And big values: on legal input, the largest k plus i the code ever computes is one billion and one, that's ten to the ninth plus one. It's well below int max, which is about two point one billion. Why so small? The loop returns at the first missing key, so it never walks far past the largest card. The undefined-behavior and address sanitizers are both clean. Both official examples pass. I also checked the code against exhaustive backtracking on two hundred seventy thousand, five hundred ninety-two cases, with zero mismatches.

Let me think about complexity here. The inner loop sits inside the outer loop, so it looks like n times g. It's not. Every inner step that passes subtracts count, and count is at least one. The total I can subtract is at most n, the number of cards. Plus at most one failing step before I return. So the inner loop runs at most n plus one times in total. At n equals ten thousand, the most I saw was ten thousand and one. The time complexity is n log n. Building the map is n inserts at log n each, and that part dominates. The inner steps are also map lookups, but there are at most n plus one of them. The space complexity is linear, for the map — one entry per distinct value. In the worst-case scenario, all values are distinct, so the map has n keys and every access costs log n. That's still n log n. At ten thousand cards, it runs in about three milliseconds. Oh, one more thing — this code doesn't check whether n is divisible by group size up front. It's still correct without it, because a bad size always ends up with a short group. But adding a one-line check at the top — if the hand size mod group size isn't zero, return false — is a cheap, optional early exit.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You planted the greedy fact early: the smallest card must start a group, so you start all of those groups at once. You explained why the count has to be a copy, since v becomes zero the moment you subtract at i equals zero — and why the zero-skip is needed. And you showed the nested loop is really n plus one steps in total, not n times g. Good work.
